source.filename: 2023-IEEE TIE-A Soft Variable Stiffness Hand With an integrated actuating cooling system.pdf

actuation: integrated actuating–cooling system driven by a single pump without valves using differential tube diameters (3 mm inlet, 1 mm outlet)
Joule heating via embedded Ni-Cr wire for thermal actuation
constitutive_assumptions: Hyperelastic silicone chamber is modeled as incompressible (I3 = 1) and isotropic under the Yeoh strain energy function.
Second-order Yeoh strain energy function W = C10(I1 - 3) + C20(I1 - 3)^2 governs the hyperelastic deformation of the chamber.

Constant curvature assumption (for the pneumatic/baseline bending model): the chamber deforms into an arc of uniform curvature, gravity is neglected, and the silicone exhibits purely elastic deformation.
The unstretched length of the variable stiffness structure (VSS) layer (L0) is assumed to remain constant during chamber pressurization and bending.
Reinforcement fiber winding radius (h2) for radial expansion constraint is assumed to remain unchanged during bending deformation.

Axial stretching and compression along the rod are neglected in the Cosserat model (linear local velocity vl(s) = [0, 0, 1]^T) because out-of-plane bending moment of inertia Iry is much smaller than Irx, confining bending to the XOZ plane.
Distributed external torque along the rod is assumed to be zero (tau = 0).
The variable stiffness layer behaves as an elastic beam under bending deformation, with bending stiffness determined via cantilever beam deflection relations.
control_variables: Finger structural geometry and dimensions (wavelike chamber volume Vr = 10319.88 mm^3, VSS length L0 = 150 mm, 12 bending units).
Inlet tube inner/outer diameter (3 mm) and outlet tube diameter (1 mm).
Silicone rubber material properties (Silicone 605, Young's modulus = 0.98 MPa).
Ni-Cr heating wire composition and diameter (0.2 mm diameter; 80% Ni, 20% Cr).
Heating target threshold (70 °C for thermal transition tests, 60 °C for stiffness/control tests) and cooling baseline (20 °C).
Standard operating pressure during thermal characterization (fixed at 60 kPa).
Maximum allowable chamber pressure limit (60 kPa) to prevent actuator structural damage.
Microcontroller control loop sampling frequency (Arduino Mega 2560 at 20 Hz).
dependent_variables: Bending stiffness of the soft finger (Sb, Sw) in N*mm^2.
Heating time (twh, tah) and cooling time (twc, tac) of the VSS in seconds.
Total thermal cycle time of variable stiffness (heating time plus cooling time) in seconds.
Bending angle of the finger (theta) in degrees.
Bending angle error between theoretical models and experimental measurements (E_theta1, E_theta2, E_s) in degrees.
Internal fluid pressure of the finger chamber in kPa.
Payload / load-holding capacity of the soft hand across stiffness states in grams.

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: The PCL-based variable stiffness structure produces a 15-fold stiffness reduction from 10.2 x 10^4 N*mm^2 at 20 °C to 0.67 x 10^4 N*mm^2 at 60 °C.

Actuation and cooling via water in an integrated hydraulic system shortens the variable stiffness cycle time to 505 s (heating: 262.6 s, cooling: 242.4 s), compared to 3870 s for pneumatic operation (heating: 76.8 s, cooling: 3793.2 s).
Varying the hydraulic pressure between 20 kPa and 60 kPa has no significant effect on the heating or cooling durations of the VSS.

A Cosserat rod formulation accounting for distributed finger self-weight and dynamic water mass achieves an average bending angle error of 5.62° under hydraulic pressure at 60 °C, outperforming the constant curvature model error of 25.38°.
Above a bending stiffness of 4.59 x 10^4 N*mm^2, the influence of water mass becomes negligible and the predictions of Cosserat rod theory and the constant curvature model converge.
Pressurizing the finger above 60 kPa causes actuator damage, restricting the maximum achievable bending angle to under 40° in the unheated high-stiffness state.

Simultaneous closed-loop regulation of bending angle and structural stiffness is achieved using PWM-modulated MOSFET control of pump voltage and heating wire voltage with PID feedback and Kalman filtering.
Shape retention and self-locking without electrical power consumption are realized by cooling the deformed PCL structure and depressurizing the hydraulic chamber to zero pressure.
A 680 g three-fingered hand supports payloads of 410 g in the rigid state, 1680 g in the compliant state, and up to 3560 g (>5.2 times hand self-weight) when self-locked.

experimental_setup: Fabrication of the soft finger comprising a Silicone 605 wavelike chamber (12 units), inextensible strain-limiting bottom layer, radial reinforcement fiber winding, and two embedded hollow PCL cylinders supported by internal springs and mesh tubes.
Thermal actuation using embedded 0.2 mm Ni-Cr resistance wire (80% Ni, 20% Cr) driven by electric current (0 to 1 A / 0 to 0.45 A).

Valve-free hydraulic/pneumatic circulation using differential tube diameters (inlet 3 mm, outlet 1 mm) driven by a single pump to simultaneously achieve fluidic pressurization and forced internal cooling.
Cantilever beam bending deflection test bench to empirically evaluate finger bending stiffness across temperatures from 20 °C to 60 °C.
Thermal transition characterization evaluating heating and cooling profiles between 20 °C and 70 °C under water and air at varying operating pressures (20 to 60 kPa).

Electronic control system incorporating an Arduino Mega 2560 microcontroller (20 Hz sampling rate), K2232 MOSFET drivers for pump (0–11 V) and Ni-Cr wire (0–18 V) PWM control, temperature sensors, and a Kalman-filtered pressure sensor.

Three-fingered robotic hand assembled with a 3D-printed polylactic acid (PLA) frame (overall hand dimensions 260 x 175 x 175 mm, mass 680 g) tested on diverse target objects in 1-, 2-, and 3-finger grasping configurations.
future_work: Reducing the variable stiffness cycle time to under 1 minute by optimizing the thermal dissipation of the VSS.
Decreasing the wall thickness of the PCL material within the VSS.
Routing fluid flow along both the inner and outer surfaces of the hollow PCL structure to accelerate heat transfer.
Incorporating liquid metal (75.5 wt% gallium and 24.5 wt% indium) into melting PCL to synthesize high-thermal-conductivity PCL composites.
Developing adaptive control algorithms, such as fuzzy PID or radial basis function (RBF) neural networks, to avoid manual tuning of control parameters across differing experimental conditions.
independent_variables: Applied fluid pressure (ranging from 10 kPa to 60 kPa, evaluated in 10 kPa steps).
Electric heating current applied to the Ni-Cr wire (ranging from 0 to 1 A).
Temperature of the PCL material (ranging from 20 °C to 70 °C).
Target stiffness state (high stiffness ~10.2 x 10^4 N*mm^2 vs. low stiffness ~0.67 x 10^4 N*mm^2).
Robotic hand operational arrangement (one-fingered, two-fingered, or three-fingered configuration).
limitations_inferred: Actuator deformation and trajectory tracking are posture-dependent because the distributed weight of water will cause varying gravitational deflection when oriented horizontally or inverted rather than downward.

Continuous fluid pumping is required to maintain inflation pressure due to the open differential tube design (passive 1 mm outlet), which may introduce hydraulic inefficiency compared to sealed or valved systems.
The 1D beam bending formulation does not model potential non-uniform spatial temperature gradients or transient thermal hysteresis along the length of the PCL substrate during rapid transitions.
Grasp testing was restricted to quasi-static holding trials, leaving dynamic grasping stability under external accelerations or vibrations unexamined.
limitations_stated_by_authors: Internal fluid pressures exceeding 60 kPa induce actuator damage, limiting the maximum bending angle in the high-stiffness state to less than 40°.
The variable stiffness cycle time of 505 s (over 8 minutes) is long and restricts practical real-time application of the soft hand.
Polycaprolactone is a biodegradable polymer, which constrains the long-term operational durability and reliability of the VSS.

The Cosserat-based shape control method cannot dynamically regulate finger curvature during the cooling transition once self-locking is engaged; the finger must be fully reheated, unlocked, straightened, and cooled before simultaneous control can resume.
PID controller gains (kp, ki, kd) required distinct manual tuning across different tests to balance overshoot and response speed.
main_results: The soft finger achieved a 15-fold stiffness adjustment from 10.2 x 10^4 N*mm^2 at 20 °C to 0.67 x 10^4 N*mm^2 at 60 °C.

The integrated hydraulic actuating-cooling system achieved a total thermal cycle time of 505 s (heating: 262.6 s, cooling: 242.4 s), which was over 7.6 times faster than pneumatic cooling at 3870 s (heating: 76.8 s, cooling: 3793.2 s).
Cooling and heating cycle durations were virtually insensitive to hydraulic pressure changes between 20 kPa and 60 kPa.

The Cosserat rod model accurately captured the gravity deflection caused by circulating water, achieving an average bending angle error of 5.62° compared to 25.38° for the constant curvature model at 60 °C.
When bending stiffness exceeds 4.59 x 10^4 N*mm^2, the effect of internal water weight becomes negligible and both kinematic models yield equivalent results.
Simultaneous closed-loop position and stiffness regulation was experimentally demonstrated across distinct operating regimes.
Zero-power shape locking was successfully demonstrated by cooling the PCL structure while bent and releasing hydraulic pressure to zero.
The 680 g three-fingered hand lifted 410 g in the rigid state, 1680 g in the compliant state, and 3560 g in the self-locked state (>5.2 times its self-weight).
modeling_methods: Second-order Yeoh hyperelastic constitutive model for the nonlinear silicone chamber.
Virtual work principle relating fluid pressure, water chamber volume change, silicone deformation energy, and PCL bending torque to finger bending angle.
Constant curvature kinematic formulation for baseline modeling under pneumatic pressure.
Cosserat rod theory (1-D continuous rod formulation in Frenet-Serret frame) incorporating distributed finger self-weight and variable internal water mass.
Empirical linear calibration equation correcting model angle prediction error as a function of finger stiffness.
Cantilever beam deflection equation for evaluating experimental bending stiffness.
Proportional-integral-derivative (PID) control algorithm for simultaneous position and stiffness tracking.
Kalman filtering applied to pressure sensor data for signal noise reduction.
performance_metrics: Stiffness variation range and ratio: 15-fold change from 10.2 x 10^4 N*mm^2 to 0.67 x 10^4 N*mm^2.
Thermal transition cycle time: 505 s for hydraulic system vs. 3870 s for pneumatic system.
Heating and cooling durations: hydraulic heating 262.6 s and cooling 242.4 s; pneumatic heating 76.8 s and cooling 3793.2 s (20 °C to 70 °C).
Bending angle simulation accuracy: average error of 5.62° for the Cosserat model vs. 25.38° for the constant curvature model under hydraulic actuation at 60 °C.
Maximum bending angle under high stiffness (< 40° at <= 60 kPa) vs. low stiffness (120°–130°).
Grasping load capacity: 410 g (high stiffness), 1680 g (low stiffness), and 3560 g (self-locking mode).
Payload-to-self-weight ratio in self-locking mode: > 5.2 times hand self-weight (3560 g payload / 680 g hand weight).
possible_gap_implications: Although forced hydraulic cooling substantially reduces the thermal transition period compared to air cooling, an 8.4-minute cycle time remains too slow for high-frequency industrial picking, emphasizing the need for microchannel cooling or highly conductive composite phase-change materials.

The inability to actively correct or modulate trajectory during the cooling and stiffening phase identifies a control and kinematic modeling gap for variable-stiffness actuators undergoing dynamic phase transitions.

The open differential-diameter tube design avoids valve complexity but necessitates continuous pumping and fluid discharge during inflation, presenting an architectural tradeoff between mechanical simplicity and fluidic efficiency.
The 60 kPa structural damage ceiling and the biodegradable nature of PCL expose durability and pressure limitations that restrict heavy-duty or harsh-environment soft manipulation tasks.
paper.research_objective: To develop a soft variable stiffness finger and three-fingered soft hand utilizing polycaprolactone (PCL) with an integrated actuating–cooling system where a single pump drives both bending actuation and accelerated fluidic cooling without valves; to formulate a Cosserat rod theory model that accounts for the changing weight of internal water to simultaneously control finger position and stiffness; and to achieve zero-energy grasp-and-hold capability via a self-locking mechanism.
paper.research_problem: Compliant materials in soft robotic grippers inherently limit payload capacity, while traditional variable stiffness mechanisms (such as tendons, granular jamming, SMAs, or SMPs) suffer from slow cooling response rates in air, added weight and mechanical complexity from auxiliary cooling loops, difficulty in maintaining deformed shapes without continuous energy consumption, and modeling inaccuracies arising from the added mass of hydraulic fluids.
paper.robot_type: soft hand (three-fingered soft hand, two and one fingered hands, soft finger)
stiffness_mechanism: polycaprolactone (PCL) phase transition / variable stiffness structure (VSS)
Joule heating via embedded Ni-Cr resistance wire
forced convective fluidic cooling using flowing water
paper.title: A Soft Variable Stiffness Hand With an Integrated Actuating–Cooling System
